content.title: Differentiability and Continuity in AP Calculus BC
content.overview: This lesson explores the relationship between differentiability and continuity. While differentiability is a stricter condition that implies continuity, the reverse is not always true. We will identify the specific conditions required for a function to be differentiable at a point and the common features that prevent differentiability.
learning_objectives: Define the relationship between differentiability and continuity.
Identify conditions where a continuous function fails to be differentiable.
Apply the definition of the derivative to verify differentiability at a point.
Solve for unknown constants to ensure a piecewise function is differentiable.

sections.title: The Differentiability-Continuity Relationship
sections.content: In calculus, differentiability at a point x = c requires that the derivative f'(c) exists. A fundamental theorem states: If a function f is differentiable at x = c, then f must also be continuous at x = c. This is a one-way implication. Continuity is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for differentiability. You can have a continuous function that is not differentiable, but you cannot have a differentiable function that is discontinuous.

sections.title: When Differentiability Fails
sections.content: A function fails to be differentiable at a point x = c if any of the following occur: 1. Discontinuity: If the function is not continuous at c, it cannot be differentiable. 2. Corner or Cusp: The one-sided limits of the difference quotient (the slopes from the left and right) are not equal. 3. Vertical Tangent: The limit of the difference quotient is infinite, resulting in a vertical slope where the derivative is undefined.

sections.title: Differentiability of Piecewise Functions
sections.content:
To ensure a piecewise function is differentiable at the transition point x = c, two conditions must be met: First, the function must be continuous at c (the left-hand limit equals the right-hand limit and the function value). Second, the left-hand derivative must equal the right-hand derivative at c. This ensures the graph is 'smooth' without a sharp turn.

![A linear sequence showing the requirements for differentiability: Continuity, then Equal One-Sided Derivatives, then Differentiability.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/91de1bbb-7974-47ff-a48e-7046318c55ef-1786526295920-247.webp)

worked_examples.question: Let f(x) be a piecewise function defined as f(x) = ax^2 + 10 for x <= 2, and f(x) = bx + 6 for x > 2. Find the values of a and b such that f(x) is differentiable at x = 2.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Ensure continuity at x = 2. The left-hand limit is a(2)^2 + 10 = 4a + 10. The right-hand limit is b(2) + 6 = 2b + 6. Set them equal: 4a + 10 = 2b + 6, which simplifies to 4a - 2b = -4, or 2a - b = -2.
Step 2: Ensure differentiability at x = 2. The derivative of the left piece is 2ax. At x = 2, this is 4a. The derivative of the right piece is b. Set them equal: 4a = b.
Step 3: Substitute b = 4a into the continuity equation: 2a - (4a) = -2. This gives -2a = -2, so a = 1.
Step 4: Solve for b: b = 4(1) = 4. Thus, a = 1 and b = 4.

common_mistakes: Assuming continuity implies differentiability (e.g., the absolute value function is continuous but not differentiable at the origin).
Forgetting to check continuity before checking the equality of one-sided derivatives in piecewise functions.
Confusing a vertical asymptote (discontinuity) with a vertical tangent (continuous but not differentiable).
exam_tips: If a question states a function is differentiable, immediately conclude it is also continuous.
On FRQs, use limit notation to show that the left-hand derivative equals the right-hand derivative when justifying differentiability.
Look for 'sharp turns' in graphs; these are visual indicators of non-differentiability despite continuity.
content.recap: Differentiability is a 'stronger' property than continuity. For a function to be differentiable at a point, it must be continuous and have a unique, finite tangent slope (no corners, cusps, or vertical tangents). In piecewise functions, both the function values and the derivative values must match at the boundary.

knowledge_claims.content: If a function f is differentiable at x = c, then f is continuous at x = c.
Continuity at a point does not guarantee differentiability at that point.
A function is non-differentiable at a corner or cusp because the one-sided derivatives are not equal.
A function is non-differentiable at a point where the tangent line is vertical.
To verify differentiability of a piecewise function at a point, one must check both continuity and the equality of one-sided derivatives.
Differentiability at x = c requires the limit of the difference quotient [f(c+h)-f(c)]/h to exist and be finite as h approaches 0.
Visually, a differentiable function has a 'smooth' graph without breaks, holes, or sharp points.
A vertical asymptote represents a discontinuity, whereas a vertical tangent represents a point of continuity where the derivative is undefined.
If a function is not continuous at x = c, it is automatically not differentiable at x = c.
When solving for constants in piecewise functions, the continuity condition (LHL = RHL) must be satisfied before or alongside the differentiability condition.
The function f(x) = |x| is the standard example of a function that is continuous but not differentiable at x = 0.
Differentiability on an open interval (a, b) means the function is differentiable at every point within that interval.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Differentiability and Continuity — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Differentiability and Continuity: Differentiability implies continuity, but corners, cusps, vertical tangents, discontinuities, and unequal one-sided derivatives can prevent differentiability.
options.B: Interpreting Derivatives in Context: A contextual derivative must identify the rate, input, units, and meaning at the specified instant rather than report only a number.
options.C: Optimization and Curve Analysis: Optimization converts constraints into a one-variable objective and compares critical and endpoint values, while derivative signs organize a complete curve analysis.
options.D: Slope Fields and Solution Curves: A slope field displays the derivative prescribed at each point, and solution curves must follow those local slopes without crossing incompatible directions.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Differentiability implies continuity, but corners, cusps, vertical tangents, discontinuities, and unequal one-sided derivatives can prevent differentiability. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.
